description: How our picture of the atom changed step by step as new evidence accumulated.
content_html:
A Model That Keeps Changing

The history of atomic theory is a textbook case of how science actually works: each model served well until new experimental evidence forced scientists to revise or abandon it. No single scientist “discovered” the atom in its modern form — the picture we use today was built up over more than a century, with each breakthrough depending on the tools and questions of its time. Understanding this story helps you think like a scientist, not just remember facts.

Key Fact

The atomic model developed in stages: Dalton (solid sphere) → Thomson (plum pudding) → Rutherford (nuclear model) → Bohr (electron shells) → Chadwick (neutron discovered). Each change was driven by new experimental evidence, not by theory alone.

Dalton’s Solid Sphere (1803)

John Dalton proposed that all matter is made of tiny, indivisible particles called atoms. In his model, atoms were like tiny solid spheres — different for each element, but impossible to break apart. Dalton’s theory was based on careful measurements of the masses of reactants and products in chemical reactions (the law of definite proportions and the law of multiple proportions). At the time, it was the best explanation for why elements combine in fixed ratios.

Thomson’s Plum Pudding Model (1897)

In 1897, J.J. Thomson discovered the electron by experimenting with cathode rays — beams of particles that travelled from the negative terminal of a tube towards the positive terminal in a vacuum. He showed these particles had a negative charge and a mass far smaller than any atom. This proved that atoms were not indivisible — they contained smaller parts.

Thomson proposed the plum pudding model: the atom is a sphere of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it, like plums in a pudding. The positive charge was spread evenly throughout the sphere. This model explained why atoms were electrically neutral overall.

Rutherford’s Nuclear Model (1911)

The plum pudding model was overturned by a famous experiment. Working in Manchester, Ernest Rutherford directed Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden to fire alpha particles at a very thin sheet of gold foil (the Geiger–Marsden experiment, 1909; Rutherford’s interpretation published 1911). According to the plum pudding model, the alpha particles should have passed straight through with minimal deflection — positive charge was spread out, so it could not exert a strong force.

Most alpha particles did pass straight through the gold foil — suggesting that most of the atom is empty space. However, a small number were deflected at large angles, and a very few bounced almost straight back. Rutherford famously described this as “almost as incredible as if you fired artillery shells at tissue paper and they came back and hit you.”

The only explanation consistent with these results was that almost all the mass of the atom, and all its positive charge, was concentrated in an extremely small, dense region at the centre: the nucleus. The electrons orbit this nucleus, and most of the atom is empty space between the nucleus and the electrons. This replaced the plum pudding model.

Bohr’s Shell Model (1913)

Rutherford’s model had a problem: electrons orbiting a nucleus should, according to classical physics, lose energy and spiral into the nucleus. The atom should be unstable. Niels Bohr solved this by proposing that electrons do not orbit freely — they can only exist in specific energy levels (called shells or orbits). Electrons can move between levels by absorbing or emitting energy, but within a level they do not radiate energy. This explained the stability of atoms and also accurately predicted the spectrum of light emitted by hydrogen atoms.

Key Fact

Bohr’s key addition was that electrons occupy fixed energy levels (shells). Electrons can jump to a higher shell by absorbing energy and drop to a lower shell by emitting energy (as light). This is why each element produces a unique spectrum of light.

Chadwick and the Neutron (1932)

One loose end remained: the mass of atoms was always greater than could be accounted for by protons alone. In 1932, James Chadwick bombarded beryllium with alpha particles and detected a previously unknown neutral particle with a mass similar to a proton. He had discovered the neutron. This completed the picture of the nucleus as containing both protons and neutrons, explaining why atoms of the same element can have different masses (isotopes).

Each model in this story was the best available explanation of the evidence at the time. No model was abandoned because someone decided it was wrong — each was replaced only when new experimental evidence (cathode rays, alpha scattering, emission spectra, neutron bombardment) could not be explained by the existing model. This is how science should work: models are provisional and open to revision. The fact that today’s atomic model is also more complex than Bohr’s (electrons are described as probability clouds, not fixed orbits) shows that the process continues.
exam_tip_html: Questions on the history of atomic models almost always ask you to explain the change — not just name the new model, but say what evidence forced the revision. For example, “Rutherford’s nuclear model replaced the plum pudding model because most alpha particles passed straight through (showing the atom is mostly empty space) but a small number were deflected at large angles (showing a dense, concentrated positive charge at the centre).” Naming the result is worth one mark; explaining what it means for atomic structure is worth the rest. Dates are commonly tested: Dalton 1803, Thomson 1897, Rutherford experiment 1909 (published 1911), Bohr 1913, Chadwick 1932.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Atomic models developed in stages driven by experimental evidence: Dalton (solid sphere) → Thomson (plum pudding, 1897) → Rutherford (nuclear model, 1911) → Bohr (electron shells, 1913) → Chadwick (neutron, 1932).
  • Rutherford’s gold foil experiment showed that most of the atom is empty space, with a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at the centre — overturning Thomson’s plum pudding model.
  • Each model was replaced only when new evidence could not be explained by the previous model, demonstrating how scientific knowledge develops and is revised over time.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following describes the 'plum pudding' model of the atom?
A) A tiny, dense nucleus surrounded by electrons in fixed energy levels
B) A positively charged sphere with electrons embedded throughout it
C) A solid, indivisible sphere with no internal structure
D) A nucleus containing protons and neutrons with electrons orbiting freely
practice_questions.marks: B) A positively charged sphere with electrons embedded throughout it [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the name of the experiment that provided evidence for the nuclear model of the atom, and who carried it out.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The Geiger–Marsden (gold foil / alpha scattering) experiment (1) carried out by Geiger and Marsden under Rutherford's direction / by Rutherford (1).
Secure: Names gold foil experiment and Rutherford.
Developing: Names either the experiment or the scientist.
Emerging: No creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Describe what happened in the gold foil experiment and explain what this showed about the structure of the atom.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Most alpha particles passed straight through (1) showing the atom is mostly empty space; a small number were deflected at large angles (1) showing there is a concentrated positive charge at the centre; this tiny, dense centre is the nucleus (1).
Secure: Two observations with correct interpretation.
Developing: States particles passed through or were deflected but does not fully interpret.
Emerging: Vague description of the experiment.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the development of the atomic model from Dalton to Bohr is an example of how scientific knowledge develops over time.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Each model was accepted as the best explanation of available evidence at the time (1); Dalton's solid sphere was replaced when Thomson discovered electrons (1); Thomson's plum pudding was replaced when Rutherford's alpha scattering results could not be explained by a diffuse positive charge (1); Bohr modified Rutherford's model when it could not explain why electrons didn't lose energy and spiral inward (1); models are revised only when new evidence forces revision — they are not discarded arbitrarily (1).
Secure: Four points with clear sense of evidence driving change.
Developing: Two to three changes described with partial explanation.
Emerging: Names scientists without explaining the process.

practice_questions.text: Compare the Rutherford nuclear model and the Bohr model of the atom. What problem did Bohr's model solve that Rutherford's could not?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both models have electrons orbiting a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus (1); Rutherford's model does not specify where electrons can orbit (1); Bohr proposed electrons occupy fixed energy levels (shells) and do not emit energy within a level (1); this solved the problem of why electrons don't spiral into the nucleus under classical physics (1).
Secure: Three points with correct comparison.
Developing: Describes one model adequately.
Emerging: Names both models without comparison.

practice_questions.text: Explain how James Chadwick's discovery of the neutron in 1932 completed the nuclear model of the atom.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Before 1932, the nucleus was thought to contain only protons (1); the mass of most atoms was greater than could be explained by protons alone (1); Chadwick discovered a neutral particle (the neutron) with a mass similar to a proton, which accounted for the extra mass and completed the picture of the nucleus containing both protons and neutrons (1).
Secure: Problem and solution both addressed.
Developing: States neutron was discovered and adds to nucleus but does not explain the mass problem.
Emerging: Names neutron without explaining its significance.

knowledge_checks.q: Who proposed the 'plum pudding' model of the atom?
What did the large-angle deflection of alpha particles in the gold foil experiment indicate?
options: The atom is a solid sphere with no internal structure.
Electrons are embedded throughout a positive sphere.
The positive charge and mass of the atom are concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus.
Electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed energy levels.

knowledge_checks.q: Bohr proposed that electrons occupy fixed _____ around the nucleus, explaining why atoms are stable.
The neutron was discovered by James Chadwick in _____.
Match each scientist to their contribution to atomic theory:
right: Proposed atoms are tiny, solid, indivisible spheres
Showed atoms have a tiny, dense, positive nucleus with mostly empty space
Proposed electrons orbit in fixed energy levels (shells)

flashcard_questions.q: What did Dalton propose about atoms in 1803?
flashcard_questions.a: That atoms are tiny, solid, indivisible spheres — different for each element.

flashcard_questions.q: Who discovered the electron and when?
What is the plum pudding model?
flashcard_questions.a: A positive sphere with electrons embedded throughout, like plums in a pudding.

flashcard_questions.q: What experiment overturned the plum pudding model?
What did most alpha particles do in the gold foil experiment?
flashcard_questions.a: Passed straight through, showing most of the atom is empty space.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the deflection of some alpha particles prove?
flashcard_questions.a: That a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus exists at the atom's centre.

flashcard_questions.q: In what year did Rutherford publish his nuclear model?
What did Bohr add to Rutherford's model?
flashcard_questions.a: Electrons occupy fixed energy levels (shells) and do not spiral inward.

flashcard_questions.q: What subatomic particle did James Chadwick discover in 1932?
Why was the neutron's discovery important?
flashcard_questions.a: It explained why atomic masses are greater than proton numbers alone.

flashcard_questions.q: The nucleus contains which two types of subatomic particle?
What is the relative charge and relative mass of an electron?
flashcard_questions.a: Charge −1, mass approximately negligible (roughly 1 over 1836 of a proton's mass).

glossary_terms.definition: English chemist (1766–1844) who proposed the first modern atomic theory: that all matter is made of tiny, indivisible, solid spheres called atoms.
A negatively charged subatomic particle, much lighter than a proton or neutron, that orbits the nucleus in energy levels; discovered by J.J. Thomson in 1897.
Thomson's 1897 model of the atom: a positively charged sphere with negatively charged electrons embedded in it, like plums in a pudding.
New Zealand-born physicist (1871–1937) whose gold foil experiment demonstrated that atoms have a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus.
Positively charged particles identical to helium nuclei, used by Rutherford to probe atomic structure in the gold foil experiment.
The tiny, dense, positively charged core of an atom, containing protons and neutrons; discovered through Rutherford's alpha-scattering experiment.
Danish physicist (1885–1962) who proposed in 1913 that electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed energy levels and can only gain or lose energy by jumping between levels.
Fixed shells around the nucleus in which electrons can exist without radiating energy; the concept was proposed by Niels Bohr in 1913.
A subatomic particle with no electric charge and a relative mass of 1, found in the nucleus; discovered by James Chadwick in 1932.
